security.meta.title: Security & Privacy - encrypt.click
security.meta.description: How encrypt.click handles data: browser-side crypto, encrypted chat and transfers, what third parties see, and what we do not collect.
security.subtitle: A plain-language summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle your data. For information only - not legal advice.
security.noAccounts.title: No accounts, no logins
security.noAccounts.text: encrypt.click has no user accounts, logins, or profiles. You do not need to register or provide personal information to use the tools.
security.clientSide.title: Browser-side tools
security.clientSide.p1: Developer and privacy tools, including hashing, key generation, encoding, and other local utilities, run in your browser using Web Crypto and other browser APIs. Their inputs are not uploaded to encrypt.click for processing.
security.clientSide.p2: When a tool requests public data at your direction, such as drand randomness for Time Capsule through our same-origin proxy, the request does not include your plaintext secrets or passwords.
security.shortening.title: Link shortening
security.shortening.p1: After encryption, your browser sends the share link to /api/shorten on encrypt.click, which shortens it with our own service at l.encrypt.click. No third-party shorteners are used. If shortening fails, you get the full link instead.
security.shortening.p2: The short link stores the full link including the encrypted payload, but never the password. Anyone with the short link still needs the password, so use the generated passphrase or another strong password.
security.shortening.p3: The full link keeps the payload in the URL fragment, which never leaves your browser. Share it instead of the short link if you don't want the encrypted payload stored on l.encrypt.click.
security.cookies.title: Cookies and browser storage
security.cookies.p1: The site sets one functional cookie, ec-lang, only after you pick a language in the menu. It holds the two-letter language code, nothing else, for one year, and is not used for tracking. The first visit without it is served in your browser language. Your browser may use localStorage for the theme and, when local chat history is enabled, encrypted message envelopes on your device. Session storage may briefly hold a room password while you join.
security.cookies.p2: Cloudflare (hosting) may set cookies for security and abuse prevention depending on traffic and browser settings, under Cloudflare's own policies.
security.network.title: Network and transport security
security.network.li1: All traffic is served over HTTPS with modern TLS.
security.network.li2: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is enabled with includeSubDomains and preload.
security.network.li3: Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts scripts, styles, fonts, and connections; inline script hashes are used instead of broad unsafe-inline for scripts.
security.network.li4: Framing is disabled via frame-ancestors 'none' and X-Frame-Options: DENY.
security.thirdParty.title: Third-party infrastructure
security.thirdParty.p1: The site runs on Cloudflare Workers. Real-time chat and the whiteboard are relayed by Durable Objects in the same Worker (PartyServer). Calls may be relayed through Cloudflare TURN or another configured TURN provider. Temporary ciphertext hosts, including Send-compatible instances, may receive encrypted blobs when first-party upload is unavailable.
security.thirdParty.p2: encrypt.click does not maintain a database of your tool inputs. API abuse controls use a salted hash of the IP address held in memory for about 60 seconds. Cloudflare may also apply bot detection or challenges under its own policies.
security.disclosure.title: Responsible disclosure
security.disclosure.text: If you believe you found a security or privacy issue in encrypt.click, email mail@encrypt.click. Include enough detail to reproduce the issue and avoid testing that could impact other users.
security.nonLegal.title: Non-legal summary
security.nonLegal.text: This page is a human-readable summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle data. It is not a contract or a complete set of legal terms. Perfect security cannot be guaranteed; you use the tools at your own risk.

tools.about.title: How it works
tools.aesWords.about.1.title: What it does
tools.aesWords.about.1: AES words encrypts a message with a password and then writes the encrypted bytes out as a list of words instead of an unreadable string of letters and symbols. The words are easier to copy by hand, dictate over the phone or paste into places that mangle special characters. Paste the same words back in with the same password and you get the original message.
tools.aesWords.about.2.title: The encryption
tools.aesWords.about.2: Your password is stretched with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations and a random 16-byte salt into a 256-bit key. The message is then encrypted with AES-256-GCM and a random 12-byte nonce. AES (originally called Rijndael, designed by the Belgian cryptographers Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen) won a public NIST competition in 2000 and has protected everything from banking to TLS since. GCM mode also authenticates the data, so a wrong password or a single changed word makes decryption fail instead of producing garbage.
tools.aesWords.about.3.title: Bytes to words
tools.aesWords.about.3: The encrypted result is split into 14-bit pieces and each piece picks one word from a fixed list of exactly 16,384 Czech words. The idea is old: the PGP word list from 1995 read key fingerprints aloud as words, and Bitcoin wallets use BIP-39 phrases with 2,048 words. Expect at least 32 words even for a very short message, because the salt, nonce and authentication tag always travel along.
tools.aesWords.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.aesWords.about.4: Everything runs in your browser and nothing is sent to encrypt.click. The words are ciphertext, not a password, so anyone who sees them can try to guess your password offline. The 600,000 iterations slow that down, but a short or common password can still fall, so use a long passphrase. Words must match exactly, including Czech diacritics such as ě or ř, and their order matters.
tools.base64.about.1.title: What it does
tools.base64.about.1: Base64 turns any text into a string made only of the letters A to Z and a to z, the digits 0 to 9 and the characters + and /, with = as padding. Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, so the result is about a third longer. This tool encodes your text as UTF-8 first, so accents and emoji survive the round trip.
tools.base64.about.2.title: Where it comes from
tools.base64.about.2: Early email could only carry plain 7-bit text, so attachments and non-English characters had to be dressed up as safe characters. Base64 appeared in Privacy-Enhanced Mail in the late 1980s, became part of MIME in 1992 and is defined today in RFC 4648. You meet it in email attachments, data: URLs, PEM keys, HTTP Basic authentication and JSON Web Tokens.
tools.base64.about.3.title: It is not encryption
tools.base64.about.3: Base64 hides nothing. There is no key, and anyone can decode it in a second, so never use it to protect a password or a secret. The conversion runs entirely in your browser. Decoding expects standard Base64; the URL-safe variant with - and _ is not accepted here, and binary data that is not valid text shows up with replacement characters.
tools.bcrypt.about.1.title: What it does
tools.bcrypt.about.1: Bcrypt turns a password into a one-way hash that can be stored in a database and later used to check whether someone typed the right password. You can create a hash here, or paste an existing one and test a password against it. A hash cannot be turned back into the password.
tools.bcrypt.about.2.title: Slow on purpose
tools.bcrypt.about.2: Niels Provos and David Mazières presented bcrypt in 1999. It builds on Bruce Schneier's Blowfish cipher and deliberately makes its key setup expensive. The cost factor (4 to 15 here, 10 by default) is a power of two: every step up doubles the work, both for your server and for an attacker trying billions of guesses. A random 16-byte salt makes every hash unique, so two people with the same password get different hashes.
tools.bcrypt.about.3.title: Reading a hash
tools.bcrypt.about.3: A result like $2b$10$… contains everything needed to verify it: the version (2b), the cost (10), a 22-character salt and the 31-character hash itself. That is why verification only needs the hash and the password.
tools.bcrypt.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.bcrypt.about.4: Hashing and verification run in your browser through WebAssembly; nothing is uploaded. Bcrypt only looks at the first 72 bytes of a password and ignores the rest. It is still a solid choice, although newer designs such as Argon2id, the 2015 Password Hashing Competition winner, are recommended for new systems. Bcrypt is for checking passwords, not for encrypting data you need to get back.
tools.hmac.about.1.title: What it does
tools.hmac.about.1: HMAC creates a signature for a message using a secret key that both sides share. The receiver computes the same HMAC and compares: if they match, the message really came from someone who knows the key and was not changed on the way. This tool uses HMAC-SHA256 and shows the result as 64 hexadecimal characters.
tools.hmac.about.2.title: Where it comes from
tools.hmac.about.2: Mihir Bellare, Ran Canetti and Hugo Krawczyk designed HMAC in 1996; it was published as RFC 2104 a year later. Simply hashing a key together with a message can be broken in surprising ways, and HMAC's two nested hash passes close those holes. Today it signs webhooks from services like GitHub and Stripe, protects API requests and is the HS256 algorithm in JSON Web Tokens.
tools.hmac.about.3.title: Good to know
tools.hmac.about.3: Signing happens in your browser with Web Crypto, and neither the key nor the message leaves your device. HMAC proves integrity, not secrecy: the message itself stays readable. Anyone who has the key can create valid signatures, so a leaked key means forged messages. The key is used exactly as typed, as UTF-8 text, so make sure both sides encode it the same way.
tools.jwt.about.1.title: What it does
tools.jwt.about.1: A JSON Web Token is three Base64url parts joined by dots: a header that names the algorithm, a payload with claims such as user ID or expiry, and a signature. This tool decodes the header and payload so you can read them, which is handy when debugging login and API problems.
tools.jwt.about.2.title: Where it comes from
tools.jwt.about.2: JWT was standardized as RFC 7519 in 2015, together with the wider JOSE family for signing and encrypting JSON. Times in claims such as exp, iat and nbf are Unix timestamps in seconds. A normal signed JWT is not encrypted: anyone holding the token can read the payload, exactly as this tool does.
tools.jwt.about.3.title: Good to know
tools.jwt.about.3: Decoding runs only in your browser; the token is not sent anywhere. This tool does not verify the signature, so it cannot tell you whether a token is genuine. Verification needs the issuer's key and belongs on your server. Treat real tokens like passwords: anyone who has a valid one can usually act as that user until it expires.
tools.pgpKeys.about.1.title: What it does
tools.pgpKeys.about.1: This tool creates an OpenPGP key pair with your name and email. Share the public key so people can encrypt messages to you and check your signatures. Keep the private key to yourself; it decrypts those messages and signs in your name. The keys work with GnuPG, Thunderbird, Proton Mail, Kleopatra and other OpenPGP software.
tools.pgpKeys.about.2.title: A bit of history
tools.pgpKeys.about.2: Phil Zimmermann released Pretty Good Privacy in 1991 so that ordinary people could encrypt email. Because strong cryptography counted as a munition under US export rules, he spent three years under criminal investigation until the case was dropped in 1996. PGP became the open standard OpenPGP (RFC 4880, updated as RFC 9580 in 2024), and the free GnuPG implementation followed in 1999.
tools.pgpKeys.about.3.title: How the keys are made
tools.pgpKeys.about.3: Keys are generated in your browser with the openpgp.js library, version 6. You can choose RSA with 2048 or 4096 bits; 4096 is the default. Nothing is uploaded. If you enter a passphrase, the private key is stored encrypted with it; without one, the private key file is unprotected and anyone who gets the file can use it.
tools.pgpKeys.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.pgpKeys.about.4: Back up the private key somewhere safe and offline. If you lose it, you can no longer read messages encrypted to you, and nobody can recover it for you. If it leaks, publish a revocation and create a new key. Modern OpenPGP tools also offer smaller and faster elliptic-curve keys; this tool sticks to RSA for the widest compatibility.
tools.photoCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.photoCipher.about.1: Photo cipher hides an encrypted message inside an ordinary photo in a way designed to survive moderate JPEG recompression, which is what chat apps and social networks do to images. The person who receives the photo opens it here with the same password and gets the message back.
tools.photoCipher.about.2.title: How the message is hidden
tools.photoCipher.about.2: The photo is split into 8×8 pixel blocks, the same grid JPEG works on. Each block carries one bit by nudging its average brightness to the nearest even or odd step on a scale of 24 levels, a technique called quantization index modulation that Brian Chen and Gregory Wornell described around 1998. JPEG compression keeps the average brightness of a block quite well, so the bits tend to survive. Every bit is written 7 times in blocks spread across the picture, and a majority vote corrects damaged copies.
tools.photoCipher.about.3.title: Encryption and capacity
tools.photoCipher.about.3: Before hiding, the message is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key derived from your password with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations). The photo is scaled so that its sides are between 800 and 2,048 pixels. Capacity is small: an 800×800 photo holds roughly 118 characters, and larger photos hold more.
tools.photoCipher.about.4.title: Limits
tools.photoCipher.about.4: Resizing, cropping, filters, brightness changes or very strong compression destroy the hidden data, and some apps downscale large photos automatically. Send the photo as a file when you can and test it first. The brightness changes may show up as faint blockiness on smooth areas such as sky. The hiding pattern is public, so anyone with this tool can tell that a photo carries data; only the content is protected, by your password. Everything runs in your browser and the photo is not uploaded.
tools.rsa.about.1.title: What it does
tools.rsa.about.1: This tool generates an RSA key pair: a public key you can give to anyone and a private key that only you keep. Data encrypted with the public key can only be opened with the private key, and a signature made with the private key can be checked by anyone with the public key.
tools.rsa.about.2.title: A bit of history
tools.rsa.about.2: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman published RSA at MIT in 1977. It later emerged that Clifford Cocks at the British GCHQ had found the same idea in 1973, but it stayed classified until 1997. RSA's security rests on how hard it is to factor the product of two huge primes; the patent expired in 2000 and RSA has been everywhere since, from TLS certificates to code signing.
tools.rsa.about.3.title: What you get
tools.rsa.about.3: Keys are generated by your browser's Web Crypto API with the public exponent 65537. You get the public key as a standard SPKI PEM file and the private key as a PKCS#8 PEM file. The private key is not encrypted, so store it in a password manager or an encrypted drive. Choose 2048 bits or more: 1024-bit keys are considered too weak today and are offered only for testing.
tools.rsa.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.rsa.about.4: Nothing is uploaded; the keys exist only in this page until you copy them. Anyone who gets the private key can decrypt your data and sign as you. RSA would be broken by a large enough quantum computer, which is why new standards for post-quantum cryptography are being rolled out.
tools.spectralCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.spectralCipher.about.1: Spectral cipher draws a picture into sound. It turns an image into a WAV file that sounds like noise, but when you open the audio in a spectrogram viewer, which plots frequencies over time, the picture appears. The reveal mode does the reverse and extracts the image from such a WAV file.
tools.spectralCipher.about.2.title: A musical trick
tools.spectralCipher.about.2: Musicians have hidden images in spectrograms for decades. Aphex Twin put his own grinning face into a track on the 1999 Windowlicker single, Nine Inch Nails hid images in the Year Zero album in 2007, and Mick Gordon tucked pentagrams and the number 666 into the 2016 Doom soundtrack.
tools.spectralCipher.about.3.title: How it works
tools.spectralCipher.about.3: The image is resized to 512×512 pixels and turned to grayscale. Each column becomes a short slice of sound of about 46 ms, and each row becomes a frequency between 300 Hz and 14 kHz whose loudness follows the brightness of the pixel. The result, about 24 seconds long, is mixed into a carrier track; the strength slider sets how strongly the image stands out against it.
tools.spectralCipher.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.spectralCipher.about.4: This is a hidden picture, not encryption. There is no password, and anyone who opens the file in a spectrogram viewer such as Audacity will see the image. Use it for puzzles, art and fun, not for secrets. MP3 and AAC compression, resampling or trimming the start can blur or shift the image, so share the WAV as it is. Everything runs in your browser.
tools.sshKeys.about.1.title: What it does
tools.sshKeys.about.1: This tool creates an RSA key pair for SSH, so you can log in to servers or push to Git hosts like GitHub and GitLab without typing a password. Put the public key on the server or in your account settings, and keep the private key on your computer.
tools.sshKeys.about.2.title: A bit of history
tools.sshKeys.about.2: In 1995 Tatu Ylönen, a researcher at the Helsinki University of Technology, saw a password-sniffing attack on his university network and wrote SSH to replace insecure tools such as Telnet and rlogin. The free OpenSSH project from OpenBSD followed in 1999 and is now built into nearly every server, Mac and Windows computer.
tools.sshKeys.about.3.title: What you get
tools.sshKeys.about.3: Keys are generated in your browser with Web Crypto, RSA with 2048 or 4096 bits. The public key comes as a single ssh-rsa line ready for authorized_keys. The private key comes as a PKCS#8 PEM file, which OpenSSH reads directly. It has no passphrase; you can add one later with ssh-keygen -p -f yourkey, and you should.
tools.sshKeys.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.sshKeys.about.4: Nothing is uploaded. The private key file must be readable only by you, otherwise ssh refuses it (on Linux and macOS: chmod 600). Modern OpenSSH prefers Ed25519 keys, which are shorter and faster; RSA keys still work everywhere and remain a safe choice at 2048 bits and above. If a computer with your key is lost or compromised, remove the public key from every server and account.
tools.steganography.about.1.title: What it does
tools.steganography.about.1: This tool hides an encrypted message inside a PNG image. The picture looks the same to the eye, but someone with the password can pull the message back out here. It is handy when you want a secret to travel as an innocent-looking image.
tools.steganography.about.2.title: An ancient idea
tools.steganography.about.2: Steganography means covered writing in Greek. Herodotus tells of Histiaeus, who around 500 BC shaved a slave's head, tattooed a message on the scalp and sent him off once the hair had grown back. The German abbot Johannes Trithemius gave the craft its name in his book Steganographia, written in 1499. Invisible ink and microdots continued the tradition, and digital images are its modern form.
tools.steganography.about.3.title: How it works
tools.steganography.about.3: The message is first encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with a key derived from your password with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations). The encrypted bits are then written into the least significant bit of the red, green and blue values of each pixel, starting at the top left. Changing a colour value by one out of 255 is invisible. Each pixel holds 3 bits, so even a small image can carry a long message.
tools.steganography.about.4.title: Limits
tools.steganography.about.4: The hidden data survives only an exact copy of the PNG file. Any resizing, cropping, editing or conversion to JPEG, which most chat apps and social networks do, wipes it out; send the file as a document or attachment, or use Photo cipher instead. The method is simple, and statistical tools can detect that an image carries data, even though they cannot read it without the password. Everything runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
tools.timeCapsule.about.1.title: What it does
tools.timeCapsule.about.1: Time capsule locks a message until a moment you choose. Before that time nobody can open it: not the recipient, not you and not encrypt.click. Afterwards, anyone with the capsule can. It suits sealed predictions, delayed reveals, contest answers or a letter to your future self.
tools.timeCapsule.about.2.title: drand and the League of Entropy
tools.timeCapsule.about.2: The lock is opened by drand, a public randomness beacon that grew out of research at the Swiss university EPFL. Since 2019 it has been run by the League of Entropy, a group of independent organisations that agreed to operate it together. Founders included Cloudflare, Protocol Labs, Kudelski Security, the University of Chile and EPFL, and today the network includes the Ethereum Foundation, University College London and more than a dozen others. Every 3 seconds the members jointly produce a threshold BLS signature for the next round number. No single member, and no small group of them, can create it alone or ahead of time.
tools.timeCapsule.about.3.title: How the lock works
tools.timeCapsule.about.3: Your chosen time is converted to a future drand round. The message is encrypted in your browser with tlock, a scheme published by drand researchers in 2023: identity-based encryption on the BLS12-381 curve, where the round number is the identity and the beacon's future signature for that round is the only key that opens it. Inside, the message is packed in the age format and sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Encrypting needs nothing secret from anyone; decrypting needs the signature, which does not exist until the round arrives.
tools.timeCapsule.about.4.title: A short history of timelocks
tools.timeCapsule.about.4: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and David Wagner proposed time-lock puzzles in 1996: problems that take a known amount of sequential computing to solve. Rivest's LCS35 puzzle, set at MIT in 1999 and expected to take 35 years, was cracked in 2019 by the Belgian programmer Bernard Fabrot after three and a half years of computing on a home PC. Puzzles like that depend on how fast computers get. tlock depends on a clock run by many organisations instead, so the unlock time is accurate to a few seconds.
tools.timeCapsule.about.5.title: Good to know
tools.timeCapsule.about.5: There is no password. After the unlock time, anyone with the capsule can read it, and the unlock time itself is visible inside the capsule. Your browser reaches drand through encrypt.click's server, which forwards requests to api.drand.sh. It sees which round is requested, never your message, and your browser checks every beacon's signature, so the server cannot fake one. If drand shut down before your round, the capsule could never be opened. Opening early would require a large share of the League's members to collude. The scheme is not resistant to future quantum computers.
chat.about.1.title: How to start
chat.about.1: Pick a room name and share the link with the people you want to talk to. Without a password, the room key is a random 256-bit secret placed after the # in the link; that part of a URL is never sent to any server, so the whole link is the key. With a password of at least 12 characters, the link no longer carries the key and everyone has to type the password, which you should share another way, for example in person or over a different app.
chat.about.2.title: Messages
chat.about.2: Every message is encrypted in your browser with AES-256-GCM. The key is derived from the link secret or password with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations. From the same secret, the browser derives a second, separate value that only proves to the server that you belong in the room. The server learns that value, never the encryption key, and the room on the server is named after a hash of it rather than after your room name.
chat.about.3.title: What the server sees and keeps
chat.about.3: Rooms run on Cloudflare Workers. The relay forwards encrypted messages to the people in the room and does not store them. It keeps only the room settings, and deletes them when the room has been empty for 7 days. It does see when messages are sent and roughly how big they are, how many people are connected and when someone is typing. Cloudflare, like any host, sees your IP address, and the room name appears in the page address you load.
chat.about.4.title: History and disappearing messages
chat.about.4: In the default mode each participant keeps an encrypted history in their own browser, and people who are online can pass it to newcomers. You can instead make messages disappear 10 or 5 seconds after they are shown. The timer runs in each participant's browser, so a modified client or a simple screenshot can still keep a copy.
chat.about.5.title: Calls
chat.about.5: Voice and video calls use WebRTC with standard DTLS-SRTP encryption between participants. Call setup travels through the room as encrypted messages. Media always goes through a TURN relay, so participants never see each other's IP addresses; the relay forwards encrypted packets and cannot listen in. Every participant connects to every other one, so calls work best in small groups.
chat.about.6.title: Files
chat.about.6: Files up to 50 MB are encrypted in your browser with a key derived from the room secret, including the file name. The encrypted file is uploaded to encrypt.click's own storage, or, if that fails, to backup hosts through encrypt.click's server. The hosts see only the encrypted file, its size and the uploading address. The download link travels inside an encrypted message.
chat.about.7.title: Good to know
chat.about.7: The chat is only as private as the link or password: anyone who has it can read along. A wrong password does not cause an error. It leads into a different, empty room, so if you find yourself alone where you expected others, check the password. Up to 32 people can join a room.
whiteboard.about.1.title: How to start
whiteboard.about.1: Choose a room name, keep the generated passphrase or type your own of at least 12 characters, and open the board. Send the link to your collaborators and share the password separately, ideally in person or over another app. The password is not part of the link.
whiteboard.about.2.title: Encryption
whiteboard.about.2: The password is turned into an AES-256-GCM key with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations, using the room name as salt. Every stroke, shape, text and cursor movement is encrypted in your browser before it leaves. A separate value derived from the same password lets you into the room without revealing the key to the server.
whiteboard.about.3.title: What the server sees and keeps
whiteboard.about.3: The relay on Cloudflare Workers passes encrypted updates between participants and stores nothing. The drawing lives only in the browsers of the people in the room and syncs between them as encrypted CRDT updates. When the last person leaves, the board is gone, so export a PNG if you want to keep it. The relay can see how many people are connected and when updates are sent, and Cloudflare sees IP addresses.
whiteboard.about.4.title: Good to know
whiteboard.about.4: Anyone with the room name and password can join and see everything on the board, so treat the pair like a key. Up to 32 people can draw together, and anyone in the room can lock it so that nobody new can join until they unlock it or leave.

security.chat.title: Encrypted chat, calls, whiteboard, and files
security.chat.p1: Chat messages, typing indicators, and call signaling are encrypted in the browser (AES-GCM) before they reach the relay. The relay forwards ciphertext and does not store chat message history.
security.chat.p2: Live calls use WebRTC with a TURN-only ICE policy so peer IP addresses are not exchanged directly. Media is protected by DTLS-SRTP between participants; TURN only relays encrypted packets. TURN credentials are fetched from encrypt.click (/api/turn).
security.chat.p3: Chat file attachments are encrypted client-side before upload, using the same ciphertext-first approach as Encrypt & share (first-party storage when available, otherwise server-side relay of ciphertext only).
security.chat.p4: Without a password, a random secret is stored in the link fragment. Share the full link privately; the room name alone cannot open the chat.
home.tools.title: All tools
home.tools.subtitle: Everything runs in your browser. No account, nothing to install.
security.share.title: Encrypted message and file sharing
security.share.p1: Encrypt & share runs AES-GCM in your browser before anything is uploaded. The password stays on your device unless you copy or send it yourself.
security.share.p2: Automatic upload prefers first-party ciphertext storage (upload.encrypt.click). That path is limited (about 50 MB) and availability is guaranteed for about 24 hours. If it fails, your browser posts ciphertext only to encrypt.click's upload API, which may relay server-side to temporary Send-compatible hosts. Those hosts should see ciphertext and server egress - not a direct browser upload of plaintext.
security.share.p3: Recipients open links on encrypt.click (often /u). Encrypted material may sit in the URL fragment (not sent to our servers on normal page loads) or point at uploaded ciphertext. Optional PNG wrapping can hide the share link in an image for offline handoff.
security.chat.p5: Whiteboard sessions use the same realtime infrastructure for collaborative strokes and state. Treat room access like chat: use a strong password for anything sensitive.
security.network.li5: The deployment check compares freshly fetched assets and the build manifest from this server. It cannot prove the authenticity of the code running in your browser or protect against a compromised host.
